rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A mystic reads Joseph and Benjamin's ordeal as the beloved's divinely arranged trial: God draws the chosen away from all else through love, as with Adam and Joseph's brother.
rows.anchor: من اصطفاه الله تعالى في الأزل لمحبته ومشاهدته وضع في رحله صاع ملامة الثقلين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Degrees rise continually in knowledge, but creatures' knowledge is finite while God's knowledge has no limit.
rows.anchor: نرفع درجاتهم في العلم فلا يزال السالكون يترقون في العلم وتشرب أطيار أرواحهم القدسية

rows.speaker: بعض السادات
rows.claim: Since Benjamin was innocent, God caused the brothers to accuse innocent Joseph of theft as reciprocal recompense, showing that retribution is inevitable.
rows.anchor: لما كان بنيامين بريئا مما رمى به من السرقة أنطقهم الله تعالى حتى رموا يوسف عليه السلام بالسرقة

rows.speaker: بعض العارفين
rows.claim: Joseph truly stole, but in the figurative sense of stealing lovers' minds and hearts through the primordial beauty placed in him.
rows.anchor: إنهم صدقوا بنسبة السرقة إلى يوسف عليه السلام ولكنها سرقة ألباب العاشقين وأفئدة المحبين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The mystical allusion is that God admits to intimacy only those whose hearts are ready to receive knowledge of Him.
rows.anchor: أن لانفشي أسرارنا وندني إلى حضرتنا الا من كان في قلبه استعداد قبول معرفتنا

rows.speaker: بعض الخراسانيين
rows.claim: The allusion is that God takes most severely only those who claim or report something about Him without authority to do so.
rows.anchor: انا لانأخذ من عبادنا أشد أخذ الا من ادعى فينا أو أخبر عنا ما لم يكن له الاخبار عنه

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another allusion is that God takes only one who reaches for His property and claims it as his own.
rows.anchor: الا من مد يده إلى مالنا وادعاه لنفسه

rows.speaker: أبو عثمان
rows.claim: God makes a servant His friend only when entrusted with His deposits and faithful in keeping them.
rows.anchor: انا لانتخذ من عبادنا وليا الا من ائتمناه على ودائعنا فحفظها ولم يخن فيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph would not take another in Benjamin's place because the beloved has no substitute in the law of love.
rows.anchor: لم يرض أن يأخذ بدل حبيبه أذ ليس للحبيب بديل في شرع المحبة

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: The brothers' statement that Benjamin stole is figuratively true because he secretly learned Joseph's secrets in private.
rows.anchor: انهم صدقوا بذلك لكنه سرق أسرار يوسف عليه السلام حين سمع منه في الخلوة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As the trial intensified, Jacob strengthened his hope in relief and God's wisdom.
rows.anchor: لما رأى اشتداد البلاء قوى رجاؤه بالفرج

rows.speaker: بعض العارفين
rows.claim: Jacob grieved because he had lost the vision of divine beauty reflected in Joseph's face, which he had enjoyed for a time.
rows.anchor: إن تأسفه على رؤية جمال الله تعالى من مرآة وجه يوسف عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob's eyes failed after he wept so much that he could no longer see beyond his beloved.
rows.anchor: بكى حتى أضر بعينيه وكان ذلك حتى لايرى غير حبيبه

rows.speaker: بعض العارفين
rows.claim: Adam and David retained their sight because their tears expressed repentance, whereas Jacob's grief was separation from beauty reflected in Joseph.
rows.anchor: بكاء يعقوب كان بكاء حزن معجون بألم الفراق حيث فقد تجلى جمال الحق

rows.speaker: أبو سعيد القرشي
rows.claim: Adam and David did not lose sight because they wept from fear of God; Jacob was reproached because he wept over losing a pleasure.
rows.anchor: انما لم يذهب بصرهما لأن بكاءهما كان من خوف الله تعالى فحفظا وبكاء يعقوب كان لفقد لذة

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: One possibility is that divine jealousy caused Jacob's blindness because he grieved for someone other than God, as a report of God's words to Jacob says.
rows.anchor: يمكن أن يكون ذهاب بصره عليه السلام من غيرة الله تعالى عليه حين بكى لغيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preferred mystical reading is that Jacob mourned the lost disclosure of God in Joseph; seeing the Prophet's primordial manifestation would have eclipsed that grief.
rows.anchor: واختار بعض العارفين أن ذلك الاسف والبكاء ليسا الا لفوات ما انكشف له عليه السلام من تجلى الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who tell Jacob to stop remembering Joseph misunderstand lovers, who live on the beloved's remembrance and cannot be deterred by fear of death.
rows.anchor: هذا من الجهل بأحوال العشق وما عليه العاشقون فان العاشق يتغذى بذكر معشوقه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When a lover cannot speak the beloved's name, the heart remains absorbed in remembrance; death in love is itself life for the lover.
rows.anchor: واذا لم يستطع ذكره بلسانه كان مستغرقا بذكره اياه بجنانه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob complains only to God because he knows God's jealousy for His beloveds, unlike his sons; turning wholly to God brings sufficiency and generosity.
rows.anchor: أنا لاأشكو إلى غيره فاني أعلم غيرته سبحانه وتعالى على أحبابه وأنتم لاتعلمون ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob's appeal to God may bring relief through the intimacy of speaking to the One who hears him.
rows.anchor: إنما رفع قصة شكواه إلى عالم سره ونجواه استرواحا مما يجده بتلك المناجاة

rows.speaker: ذو النون
rows.claim: A poem says that noble seekers settle gladly under God's decree and ask Him not to leave them to their own plans.
rows.anchor: إذا ارتحل الكرام اليك يوما ليلتمسوك حالا بعد حال فان رحالنا حطت رضاء بحكمك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After entrusting his pain to God, Jacob senses relief coming and tells his sons to seek Joseph and Benjamin without despairing of God's mercy.
rows.anchor: كأنه عليه السلام تنسم نسائم الفرج بعد أن رفع الأمر إلى مولاه عز وجل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brothers mention famine, though their deeper affliction, had they understood it, was separation from Joseph, which had hurt their father and family.
rows.anchor: أرادوا ضر المجاعة ولو أنهم علموا وأنصفوا لقصدوا ضر فراقك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brothers' plea teaches supplicants to approach superiors humbly, acknowledge need and shortcomings, and see any response as gracious favor rather than entitlement.
rows.anchor: تعليم آداب الدعاء والرجوع إلى الأكابر ومخاطبة السادات فمن لم يرجع إلى باب سيده بالذلة والافتقار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mystical lovers should confess the harm of separation, present their deficient deeds and little knowledge as a poor offering, and ask for nearness and the gift of vision.
rows.anchor: من أعمال معلولة وأفعال مغشوشة ومعرفة قليلة لم تحط بذرة من أنوار عظمتك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brothers' affectionate address after recognizing Joseph reflects their good opinion; recognition may also have displaced awe with kinship.
rows.anchor: خاطبوه بعد المعرفة بخطاب المودة لابخطاب التكلف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It is said that Joseph's addition, this is my brother, softened the shock and shame of sudden recognition.
rows.anchor: لتهوين حال بديهة الخجل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation is that Joseph hints their brotherhood was not genuine because true brotherhood has no estrangement.
rows.anchor: للإشارة إلى أن اخوتهم لاتعد إخوة لأن الاخوة الصحيحة مالم يكن فيها جفاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph's immediate pardon exemplifies generosity: a generous person forgives when able, and an apology is accepted among the noble.
rows.anchor: وهذا من شرائط الكرم فالكريم إذا قدر عفا

rows.speaker: شاه الكرماني
rows.claim: Whoever sees people through God's decree does not dwell on their offense; Joseph excused his brothers because he understood how destiny unfolds.
rows.anchor: من نظر إلى الخلق بعين الحق لم يعبأ بمخالفتهم ومن نظر اليهم بعينه أفنى أيامه بمخاصمتهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph sent the shirt so reunion would come gradually, since Jacob could not bear an abrupt, complete return; the same shirt that began his grief now brings joy.
rows.anchor: جعل وصاله بالتدريج فأرسل اليه بقميصه ولما كان مبدأ الهم الذي أصابه من القميص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Possible reasons Joseph did not travel to Jacob himself are the burden of a large entourage, the need to keep governing, or a divine instruction; another view says the beloved's status required the father to come.
rows.anchor: أو لأن في ذلك تعطل أمر العامة وليس هناك من يقوم به غيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says the east wind asked God to carry Joseph's scent to Jacob; God granted it, and Jacob smelled the breeze while prostrating.
rows.anchor: ريح الصبا سألت الله تعالى فقالت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is quoted as saying that the Lord sends merciful breaths in people's days and believers should expose themselves to them.
rows.anchor: إن لربكم في أيام دهركم نفحات ألا فتعرضوا لنفحات الرحمن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A realized believer detects in the heart the breeze of faith and the spirit of prior divine knowledge placed inwardly by God.
rows.anchor: المؤمن المتحقق يجد نسيم الايمان في قلبه وروح المعرفة السابقة له من الله تعالى في سره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob smelled Joseph only when reunion's appointed time approached, not when Joseph was in the nearby well; unveilings likewise occur at their destined times.
rows.anchor: وإنما وجد عليه السلام هذا الريح حيث بلغ الكتاب أجله ودنت أيام الوصال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The shirt signals the beloved's manifestation: its sacred scent restores the grieving lover's sight and clears the veil from vision.
rows.anchor: يجيء اليه بشير تجليه فيلقى عليه قميص أنسه في حضرات قدسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It is said that the shirt restored Jacob's sight because it carried the pleasure of God's manifestation from Joseph, its locus, and the scent of paradise.
rows.anchor: وجد لذة نفحة الحق تعالى منه حيث كان يوسف عليه السلام محل تجليه جل جلاله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob delayed seeking forgiveness until he could verify their repentance or obtain God's leave, avoiding a rejected intercession like Noah's for his son.
rows.anchor: إلى أن يتعرف منهم صدق التوبة أو حتى يستأذن ربه تعالى في الاستغفار لهم

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: One view says Jacob promised to seek forgiveness only after he had finished rejoicing and moved on to intercession.
rows.anchor: وعدهم الاستغفار لأنه لم يفرغ بعد من استبشاره إلى استغفاره

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another view says Joseph forgave immediately because he loved his brothers less fiercely or deemed their shame sufficient punishment, while Jacob loved them more and reproached them by waiting.
rows.anchor: لأن يعقوب كان أشد حبا لهم فعاتبهم بالتأخير ويوسف لم يرهم أهلا للعتاب

rows.speaker: غير واحد من الصوفية
rows.claim: Several Sufis call anyone who turns attention toward something besides God a polytheist; a poet even treats a stray wish for another as apostasy.
rows.anchor: من التفت إلى غير الله تعالى فهو مشرك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling people to God should rest on clear insight and knowledge, free of the ego's and Satan's opposition; a preacher must know the way and God's necessary, possible, and impossible attributes.
rows.anchor: ينبغي للداعي إلى الله تعالى أن يكون عارفا بطريق الايصال اليه سبحانه عالما بما يجب له تعالى

rows.speaker: بعض العارفين
rows.claim: One gnostic says insight outranks light because it cannot coexist with even a slight inclination toward anything besides God.
rows.anchor: البصيرة أعلى من النور لأنها لاتصح لاحد وهو رقيق الميل إلى السوى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī condemns contemporary self-appointed spiritual guides as deeply ignorant and misguided despite believing they do well.
rows.anchor: الدعاة إلى الله تعالى اليوم من هؤلاء الذين نصبوا أنفسهم إلى الارشاد بزعمهم أجهل من حمار الحكيم توما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph's story instructs gnostics, lovers, patient and truthful people; rulers to uphold justice; the pious to resist lust; servants to protect masters' honor; and the powerful to forgive offenses.
rows.anchor: وفيها أيضا عبرة للملوك في بسط العدل كما فعل يوسف عليه السلام ولأهل التقوى في ترك ما تراودهم النفس

rows.speaker: بعض الصوفية
rows.claim: A Sufi allegory maps Joseph to the prepared heart, Jacob to intellect, the brothers to outer and inner senses plus appetite, and Benjamin to practical rational faculty.
rows.anchor: يوسف بالقلب المستعد الذي هو في غاية الحسن ويعقوب بالعقل والاخوة بني العلات بالحواس الخمس الظاهرة والخمس الباطنة

rows.speaker: بعض الصوفية
rows.claim: The allegory maps Rachel to the reproaching soul, Leah to the commanding soul, the well to bodily nature, Joseph's shirt to innate preparedness, and the wolf and false blood to irascibility and its effect.
rows.anchor: وراحيل أم يوسف اللوامة وليا بالنفس الامارة والجب بعقر الطبيعة البدنية والقميص الذي ألبسه يوسف

rows.speaker: بعض الصوفية
rows.claim: It maps Jacob's blindness to dull insight; Joseph's sale to nature yielding to the spirit in the holy city; and the intellectual faculty's meanings to spiritual effusions.
rows.anchor: بكلال البصيرة وفقدان نور العقل وشراؤه من عزيز مصر بثمن بخس بتسليم الطبيعة له إلى عزيز الروح

rows.speaker: بعض الصوفية
rows.claim: It maps the Egyptian governor's wife to the reproaching soul, the torn shirt to damaged luminous virtues, the husband at the door to the spirit's light, and the witness to thought or bodily nature.
rows.anchor: وامرأة العزيز بالنفس اللوامة وقد القميص من دبر بخرقها لباس الصفة النورية

rows.speaker: بعض الصوفية
rows.claim: It maps the two prison companions to spiritual love and lower desire, wine to love's intoxication, bread to pleasures, birds to bodily powers, and the king to active intellect.
rows.anchor: والصاحبين بقوة المحبة الروحية وبهوى النفس والخمر بخمر العشق والخبز باللذات

rows.speaker: بعض الصوفية
rows.claim: It maps the cows to ranks of the soul, the cup to perception, and the herald to estimation, among other correspondences.
rows.anchor: والبقرات بمراتب النفس والسقاية بقوة الادراك والمؤذن بالوهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī calls the allegorical mapping extremely strained and unnecessary, and asks God to guide to the straight path.
rows.anchor: وطبق القصة على ماذكر وتكلف له أشد تكلف وما أغناه عن ذلك والله تعالى الهادي إلى سواء السبيل

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Reports through Mujāhid from Ibn ʿAbbās and ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥa, and from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, classify Sūrat al-Raʿd as Meccan; Ibn Jubayr argues the verse about one with Scripture's knowledge cannot be Ibn Salām because the sura is Meccan.
rows.anchor: جاء من طريق مجاهد عن ابن عباس وعلي بن أبي طلحة أنها مكية

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Other reports from Mujāhid through Ibn al-Zubayr, Ibn Jurayj, and ʿUthmān from ʿAṭāʾ, and from Qatāda, classify it as Medinan; Qatāda excepts 13:31 as Meccan.
rows.anchor: وأخرج مجاهد عن ابن الزبير وابن مردويه من طريق العوفي عن ابن عباس ومن طريق ابن جريج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further report makes the opening through the verse about a Quran moving mountains Medinan and the remainder Meccan; a report tied to Arbad and Amir supports Medinan verses 13:8–13.
rows.anchor: الآية مدني وباقيها مكي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī reconciles the reports by treating the sura as Meccan except for some verses, whose count varies by regional verse enumeration: three Kufan, four Medinan, five Basran, seven Syrian.
rows.anchor: والذي يجمع به بين الاختلاف انها مكية الا آيات منها وهي ثلاث واربعون آية في الكوفي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sura follows the previous one by elaborating the heavenly and earthly signs, expanding Joseph's monotheistic argument, consoling the Prophet, and linking their Qur'an descriptions.
rows.anchor: فأجمل سبحانه الآيات السماوية والارضية ثم فصل جل شأنه ذلك هنا أتم تفصيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Abī Shayba and al-Marwazī report that people recommended reciting al-Raʿd beside the dying because it eases death and the soul's taking; al-Ālūsī calls related reports fabricated.
rows.anchor: أنه كان يستحب اذا حضر الميت أن يقرأ عنده سورة الرعد فان ذلك يخفف عن الميت

rows.speaker: بعض المحققين
rows.claim: Some authorities parse subḥān as the verbal noun of sabbaḥa, meaning to declare God transcendent, rather than the phrase saying subḥān Allāh.
rows.anchor: مصدر سبح تسبيحا بمعنى نزه تنزيها لا بمعنى قال سبحان الله

rows.speaker: صاحب القاموس
rows.claim: The author of al-Qāmūs's commentary on al-Kashshāf's preface instead treats subḥān as a verbal noun from the shortened form sabbaḥa.
rows.anchor: وإلى هذا ذهب صاحب القاموس في شرح ديباجة الكشاف وجعل سبحان مصدر سبح مخففا

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some grammarians regard subḥān as a proper name for transcendence, detached from genitive construction and diptote because of proper-name status and its added form.
rows.anchor: وقد يستعمل علما للتنزيه فيقطع عن الإضافة لأن الأعلام لا تضاف قياسا

rows.speaker: الأعشى
rows.claim: Al-Aʿshā's line uses subḥān without an expressed genitive complement as evidence that it functions as a proper name.
rows.anchor: قد قلت لما جاءني فخره سبحان من علقمة الفاخر

rows.speaker: الرضي
rows.claim: Al-Raḍī says the usual genitive construction defeats the proper-name argument; when detached, subḥān can be tanwīn-marked or take the definite article, as poetic examples show.
rows.anchor: لا دليل على علميته لأنه أكثر ما يستعمل مضافا

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī consistently treats subḥān as a generic proper name for glorification; al-Kashf defends this because a proper name can still take a genitive complement.
rows.anchor: وظاهر كلام الزمخشري أنه علم للتسبيح دائما وهو علم جنس لأن علم الجنس كما يوضع للذوات يوضع للمعاني

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī explains subḥān's emphatic transcendence through its root sense of going far, its intensive form, and its special noun form; its suppressed verb is used only of God.
rows.anchor: من حيث الاشتقاق من السبح وهو الذهاب والابعاد في الأرض ثم ما يعطيه نقله إلى التفعيل

rows.speaker: طلحة
rows.claim: A report in al-ʿIqd al-Farīd says Ṭalḥa asked the Prophet for subḥān's meaning and was told it declares God free of every evil.
rows.anchor: سألت رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم عن تفسير سبحان الله فقال

rows.speaker: الطيبي
rows.claim: Al-Ṭībī objects that the Isrāʾ context calls for wonder at the event rather than a response to opponents' claims that would require broad transcendence.
rows.anchor: إن ذلك مما يأباه مقام الإسراء إباه العيوف الورود وهو مزيف بل معناه التعجب

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشف
rows.claim: Al-Kashf holds that transcendence and wonder can coexist, but transcendence is primary here and wonder secondary; in Sūrat al-Nūr wonder is primary.
rows.anchor: أن التنزيه لا ينافي التعجب كما توهم واعترض وجعله مدارا والتعجب تبعا ههنا هو الوجه

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Other discussions say al-Kashshāf generally rejects combining transcendence and wonder because they are distinct senses; another view denies that subḥān is a proper name at all.
rows.anchor: أنه لا يرتضى الجمع بين التنزيه والتعجب للمنافاة بينهما بل لأن كلا منهما معنى مستقل

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: One grammatical reading takes subḥān as an imperative: declare God free of every deficiency, including inability to perform what follows.
rows.anchor: نزهوا الله تعالى وبرئوه من جميع النقائص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Isrāʾ means travel by night, and asrā and sarā are equivalent; the hamza is not causative according to Abū ʿUbayda, contrary to Ibn ʿAṭiyya.
rows.anchor: والاسراء السير بالليل خاصة كالسرى فأسرى وسرى بمعنى

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the hamza is causative, with angels as an implicit object; al-Baḥr counters that this was needed only because of al-Mubarrad's claim about the preposition bāʾ.
rows.anchor: الهمزة للتعدية والمفعول محذوف أي أسرى ملائكته بعبده

rows.speaker: الليث
rows.claim: Al-Layth says asrā is used for early night and sarā for late night; most authorities make sāra general, while some restrict it to daytime.
rows.anchor: يقال أسرى لأول الليل وسرى لآخره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling Muhammad God's servant signals his complete worship and highest rank; the passage also says beloveds take pride in servitude and that this wording guards against Christian-like excess.
rows.anchor: والعبودية على ما نص عليه العارفون أشرف الأوصاف وأعلى المراتب

rows.speaker: أبو القاسم سليمان الأنصاري
rows.claim: A report says God asked Muhammad how He should honor him; Muhammad answered that honor lay in being related to Him through servitude, after which this verse was revealed.
rows.anchor: لما وصل النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم إلى الدرجات العالية والمراتب الرفيعة أوحى الله تعالى إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording also blocks exaggeration about the Prophet; al-Ālūsī says God uses servant with a pronoun referring to the divine identity only for Muhammad and contrasts his station with Moses's.
rows.anchor: في التعبير به هنا دون حبيبه مثلا سدا لباب الغلو فيه صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The genitive link between subḥān and the relative phrase presents the act of Isrāʾ as evidence of God's power, wisdom, and freedom from deficiency.
rows.anchor: من أدلة كمال قدرته وبالغ حكمته وغاية تنزهه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Laylan is an accusative time expression; its indefiniteness indicates that the journey occupied only part of the night, and Ibn Masʿūd and Ḥudhayfa read min al-layl.
rows.anchor: وفائدته الدلالة بتنكيره على تقليل مدة الاسراء وأنها بعض من أجزاء الليل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some object that indefiniteness marks a subset of nights, not part of a night; another view says it denies a whole-night journey or magnifies it. Al-Ālūsī favors the account that a definite night means its whole span while an indefinite one does not.
rows.anchor: أن تنكيره لدفع توهم أن الاسراء كان في ليال

rows.speaker: عبد القاهر
rows.claim: ʿAbd al-Qāhir's account, endorsed by a commentator citing Sībawayh and Ibn Mālik, says a definite night normally measures the full night, whereas an indefinite night does not; thus it need not be metaphorical for part of one.
rows.anchor: أن الليل والنهار إذا عرفا كانا معيارا لتعميم وظرفا محدودا

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another explanation takes indefinite laylan to mean the middle or darkest portion of the night, but the author says a forthcoming report contradicts this.
rows.anchor: وقع في وسطه ومعظمه كما يقال جاءني فلان بليل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī dismisses as poorly informed the claims that laylan merely emphasizes the journey or that isrāʾ is generalized to mean travel.
rows.anchor: للتأكيد أو تجريد الاسراء وإرادة مطلق السير منه ناشيء من قلة البضاعة

rows.speaker: أنس بن مالك
rows.claim: A sound report from Mālik ibn Ṣaʿṣaʿa says the Prophet was in the Hijr or Ḥaṭīm, between sleep and wakefulness, when a visitor opened his chest and washed his heart before the journey.
rows.anchor: بينا أنا في الحجر وفي رواية في الحطيم بين النائم واليقظان إذ أتاني آت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The continuation says Gabriel asked Michael for Zamzam water, washed the Prophet's heart three times, filled it with faith and wisdom, sealed it, and brought the Buraq for the journey.
rows.anchor: فاستخرج قلبه الشريف وغسله ثلاث مرات ثم أعاده إلى مكانه وملأه إيمانا وحكمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports locating him in the Hijr can be reconciled with reports placing him between Zamzam and the Maqām; al-masjid al-ḥarām may also mean the whole sanctuary by vicinity or because all of it is a place of worship and inviolable.
rows.anchor: الجمع بين ما ذكر من أنه عليه الصلاة والسلام كان إذ ذاك في الحجر

rows.speaker: أم هانئ
rows.claim: A report from Umm Hāniʾ says the Prophet slept in her house after evening prayer, traveled and returned that night, modeled the prophets, led them in prayer, and then told Quraysh.
rows.anchor: أخرج النسائي عن ابن عباس وأبو يعلى في مسنده والطبراني في الكبير من حديثها

rows.speaker: أبو بكر
rows.claim: When Quraysh challenged the journey, Abū Bakr affirmed that if Muhammad said it, it was true; he believed even more remote claims about revelation, earning the name al-Ṣiddīq.
rows.anchor: إن كان قال ذلك فقد صدق قالوا أتصدقه على ذلك قال إني أصدقه على أبعد من ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The report says the Prophet accurately described Jerusalem and passing caravans, including water he drank and replaced, a frightened camel, and a caravan expected at sunrise; their arrival confirmed his details but the doubters called it magic.
rows.anchor: فجلى له فطفق ينظر إليه وينعته لهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another report says Umm Hāniʾ searched for the missing Prophet, fearing Quraysh, while his clan and al-ʿAbbās sought him until he said he had gone to Jerusalem and returned that night.
rows.anchor: وفي بعض الآثار أن أم هانيء قالت فقدته صلى الله عليه وسلم وكان نائما عندي

rows.speaker: النووي
rows.claim: Reports disagree on the year: al-Nawawī's Rawḍa says ten years and three months after prophethood, his Fatāwā says years five or six, and another transmission attributes to him year twelve; Ibn Ḥazm claims consensus, while other reports put it shortly before the Hijra.
rows.anchor: فذكر النووي في الروضة أنه كان بعد النبوة بعشر سنين وثلاثة أشهر

rows.speaker: عبد الحق
rows.claim: The claim in Sharīk ibn Numayr's report that the journey preceded revelation is rejected by critics; ʿAbd al-Ḥaqq says its wording contains unexplained additions and unfamiliar expressions.
rows.anchor: وقد خطأه غير واحد في ذلك ونقل الحافظ عبد الحق في كتابه الجمع بين الصحيحين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Anas's Isrāʾ report is also transmitted by Ibn Shihāb, Thābit al-Bunānī, and Qatāda, none of whom include Sharīk's additions; hadith critics do not regard Sharīk as a strong memorizer.
rows.anchor: وقد روى حديث الإسراء عن أنس جماعة من الحفاظ المتقنين والأئمة المشهورين كابن شهاب وثابت البناني وقتادة

rows.speaker: النووي
rows.claim: The month is disputed: al-Nawawī's Fatāwā says Rabīʿ I, his Muslim commentary follows Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ for Rabīʿ II, and his Rawḍa gives Rajab; other reports say Ramadan or Shawwāl.
rows.anchor: كان في شهر ربيع الأول وقال في شرح مسلم تبعا للقاضي عياض

rows.speaker: ابن الملقن
rows.claim: A report transmitted by Ibn al-Mulaqqin from al-Wāqidī says the night was the twenty-seventh and a Saturday; another view chooses Friday for its sanctity.
rows.anchor: وكان على ما قيل الليلة السابعة والعشرين من الشهر

rows.speaker: محمد بن عمر السفيري
rows.claim: Al-Safīrī argues against Friday because Gabriel prayed Ẓuhr with the Prophet the first day after Isrāʾ; the author replies that Friday prayer may have been prescribed later or concealed in Mecca, and was first held near Medina by Asʿad ibn Zurāra.
rows.anchor: ورد بأن جبرائيل عليه السلام صلى بالنبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أول يوم بعد الإسراء الظهر

rows.speaker: ابن الأثير
rows.claim: Ibn al-Athīr calls Monday the correct night, a view also chosen by Ibn al-Munīr; other reports give the seventeenth of Rabīʿ I or twenty-seventh of Rabīʿ II and different ages.
rows.anchor: الصحيح عندي أنها كانت ليلة الاثنين واختاره ابن المنير

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority reportedly call the Isrāʾ night the most excellent night, even above Laylat al-Qadr; another view ranks it higher for the Prophet and Qadr higher for his community, which the author answers by making it best for both.
rows.anchor: وهي على ما نقل السفيري عن الجمهور أفضل الليالي حتى ليلة القدر مطلقا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although Isrāʾ night is ranked highest, no ritual worship was prescribed for it; worship on Laylat al-Qadr remains prescribed for the community.
rows.anchor: نعم لم يشرع التعبد فيها والتعبد في ليلة القدر مشروع إلى يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan says the journey happened in a dream, a position also attributed to ʿĀʾisha and Muʿāwiya, though the author doubts those attributions because they were not then in positions to report it.
rows.anchor: فعن الحسن أنه في المنام

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority hold that the Prophet traveled bodily and spiritually while awake; ruʾyā can mean waking sight, as a line by al-Rāʿī illustrates, and the servant wording includes both body and soul.
rows.anchor: وذهب الجمهور إلى أنه في اليقظة ببدنه وروحه صلى الله عليه وسلم والرؤيا تكون بمعنى الرؤية في اليقظة

rows.speaker: الواحدي
rows.claim: Al-Wāḥidī says it was only a waking night vision; al-Nawawī replies that Sharīk's wording may describe the angel's first arrival, not sleep through the whole journey.
rows.anchor: إنها رؤية اليقظة ليلا فقط

rows.speaker: القاضي أبو بكر
rows.claim: A group including Qāḍī Abū Bakr and al-Baghawī accepts reports of both forms and reconciles them as two journeys: an earlier spiritual dream before prophethood and a later bodily journey after it; al-Kashf endorses this as the sound synthesis.
rows.anchor: وذهبت طائفة منهم القاضي أبو بكر والبغوي إلى تصديق القائلين بأنه في المنام والقائلين بأنه في اليقظة

rows.speaker: المازري
rows.claim: Al-Māzarī offers a fourth synthesis: the Prophet went bodily and awake to Jerusalem, then ascended by spiritual vision; Quraysh mocked the earthly claim but not the ascent, and this is not the disembodied waking travel proposed by some mystics and philosophers.
rows.anchor: كان الإسراء بجسده صلى الله عليه وسلم في اليقظة إلى بيت المقدس فكانت رؤية عين

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most authorities say the Miʿrāj, like the Isrāʾ, involved body and spirit, and the author says this is possible; geometrical comparisons describe immense distances crossed rapidly by the sun and celestial sphere.
rows.anchor: والأكثر على أن المعراج كالإسراء بالروح والبدن ولا استحالة في ذلك

rows.speaker: الإمام الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī argues that bodies share the same essence, so any body's capacity for an accident applies to all; whatever God can do is possible for each body.
rows.anchor: ذكر الإمام في الأربعين أن الأجسام متساوية في الذوات والحقائق فوجب أن يصح على كل واحد منها

rows.speaker: البيضاوي
rows.claim: Al-Bayḍāwī argues that geometry makes rapid ascent possible because the sun's diameter is over 160 times Earth's and its rim crosses the disk in under a second; al-Ālūsī says the first premise confuses diameter with volume.
rows.anchor: والعلامة جعل ذلك نسبة القطر إلى القطر لأنه المتبادر مما بين الطرفين

rows.speaker: القطب الشيرازي
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī cites Quṭb al-Shīrāzī's calculation: the sphere moves a stated distance in one-fifteenth of an hour, and from first appearance to full sunrise the relevant movement is ten celestial minutes, about 519,600 farsakhs, not under a second.
rows.anchor: مقدار الدرجة الواحدة من مقعر الفلك الأطلس بالأميال 3953439 ميلا

rows.speaker: عبد الرحمن الكردي
rows.claim: Al-Kurdī says Bayḍāwī's second means a second of a day-minute; al-Ālūsī argues astronomical conventions distinguish clock minutes from arc minutes, so the apparent disagreement is terminological.
rows.anchor: مراد العلامة البيضاوي من الثانية الثانية الثالثة لا الثانية الأولى وهو ظاهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī says no astronomer divides the day into sixty minutes as a measure of time, and faults al-Kurdī's further calculation as erroneous, though he correctly rebuts two earlier commentators.
rows.anchor: ولم يقل بذلك أحد منهم وإنما ذكر ذلك بعضهم تسهيلا لمعرفة الكسر الزائد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The argument that all bodies are alike assumes indivisible atoms, disputed by al-Naẓẓām and philosophers; the author rejects using reassembly or dislocation as proof of impossibility because their demonstration is weak.
rows.anchor: وما ذكر من تساوي الأجسام مبني على ما قيل على تركبها من الجواهر الفردة وفيه خلاف النظام والفلاسفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī says the proof against bodily reassembly is weaker than a spider's web; the verse itself does not say Muhammad was carried, but sound reports say he rode the Buraq.
rows.anchor: إن برهانهم على ذلك أوهن من بيت العنكبوت كما بين في محله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Aqṣā is Jerusalem; it may mean the farthest mosque visited from Mecca, the farthest worship place, simply a distant destination, or a place far from impurities, though Ibn ʿAṭiyya's non-comparative reading is called unlikely.
rows.anchor: وهو بيت المقدس ووصفه بالأقصى أي الأبعد بالنسبة إلى من بالحجاز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sound report says Gabriel did not ride behind the Prophet but held the Buraq's stirrup while Michael led it; the sound view also says a ladder was set up for the ascent rather than riding the Buraq to heaven.
rows.anchor: والصحيح أنه لم يركب بل أخذ بركابه وميكائيل يقود البراق

rows.speaker: ابن كثير
rows.claim: Al-Ḥalabī says Ibn Kathīr wrongly faults those, including the author of the Hamziyya, who say the Prophet ascended on the Buraq.
rows.anchor: وهم الحافظ ابن كثير كما قال الحلبي القائلين ومنهم صاحب الهمزية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The famous story that the Jerusalem rock rose after the Prophet and remains suspended, held by angels with his footprint, is a fabrication.
rows.anchor: ومن الأكاذيب المشهورة أنه صلى الله عليه وسلم لما أراد العروج صعد على صخرة بيت المقدس

rows.speaker: العلائي
rows.claim: Al-ʿAlāʾī lists five mounts: Buraq to Jerusalem, a ladder to the first heaven, angelic wings to the seventh, Gabriel's wing to the lote tree, and the rafraf to two-bows' distance.
rows.anchor: وذكر العلائي في تفسيره أنه كان للنبي عليه الصلاة والسلام ليلة الإسراء خمسة مراكب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another account has only the Buraq and a ladder with ten landings, from the heavens to the lote tree, the place of the pens' scratching, and the Throne.
rows.anchor: وقيل لم يكن إلا البراق من المسجد الحرام إلى المسجد الأقصى والمعراج منه إلى حيث شاء الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī calls a Kashfiyya claim a fable: the spirit supposedly has subtle and elemental bodies, sheds each element at successive orbits, ascends in subtle form, then regains them on return.
rows.anchor: ولعمري إنه حديث خرافة لا مستند له شرعا ولا عقلا

rows.speaker: عبد الرحمن الدشتي
rows.claim: Al-Dashtī and al-Jāmī say ascent to the Throne was body and spirit, but beyond it only spirit; the author finds no transmitted evidence and notes the philosophical claim that no place or direction extends beyond the Throne.
rows.anchor: أن المعراج إلى العرش بالروح والجسد وإلى ما وراء ذلك بالروح فقط

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: An unnamed mystic says the event exceeds description: the omnipotent Beloved summoned His beloved, angels escorted him, and no distance or body could obstruct a luminous body; the author sees a possible leaning toward unity of being.
rows.anchor: أمر المعراج أجل من أن يكيف وماذا عسى يقال سوى أن المحب القادر الذي لا يعجزه شيء

rows.speaker: الثعلبي
rows.claim: Al-Thaʿlabī describes the Buraq lengthening its forelegs in valleys and hindlegs at ascents; the author infers that the route retained its extended distance rather than being folded.
rows.anchor: أنه إذا أتى واديا طالت يداه وقصرت رجلاه وإذا أتى عقبة طالت رجلاه وقصرت يداه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One source estimates the distance from Mecca to the place of divine communication at 300,000 years, another at 50,000, and other figures are reported.
rows.anchor: كانت المسافة من مكة إلى المقام الذي أوحى الله تعالى فيه إلى نبيه عليه الصلاة والسلام ما أوحى قدر ثلثمائة ألف سنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī surveys disputes over miraculous folding of distance for saints: some Sufis and jurists affirm it, some Ḥanafīs deny it, and others deem it impossible; opponents invoke interpenetration of atoms, while Sufis tell of time-spreading.
rows.anchor: طي مسافة على نحو ما يثبته الصوفية وبعض الفقهاء للأولياء كرامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He says this exceeds our minds, like treating eternity and endless future as one point by convention, and promises to revisit objections in the allegorical discussion.
rows.anchor: الأزل والأبد نقطة واحدة الفرق بينهما بالاعتبار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Night travel honored the Prophet through privacy and royal intimacy; other wisdoms include prophets' night blessings, better guidance, farther travel, and a more wondrous movement from darkness into pure light.
rows.anchor: وإنما أسري به صلى الله عليه وسلم ليلا لمزيد الاحتفال به عليه الصلاة والسلام فإن الليل وقت الخلوة والاختصاص

rows.speaker: ابن الجوزي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Jawzī adds that the Prophet is a lamp that is lit at night, and a full moon that travels through darkness; other reasons are known only to God.
rows.anchor: إن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم سراج والسراج لا يوقد إلا ليلا وبدر وكذا مسير البدر في الظلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse alone does not explicitly say the Prophet entered al-Aqṣā, but authentic reports establish that he did.
rows.anchor: ثم إن الآية ليست نصا في دخوله عليه الصلاة والسلام المسجد الأقصى إلا أن الأخبار الصحيحة نص في ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase about blessing around Jerusalem praises its shared sanctity as a prophets' worship place and former qibla, along with its many rivers and trees; a report also blesses the land between al-ʿArīsh and the Euphrates and singles out Palestine for sanctification.
rows.anchor: وبركته بما خص به من كونه متعبد الأنبياء عليهم السلام وقبله لهم وكثرة الأنهار والأشجار حوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says all the earth's waters spring from beneath Jerusalem's rock, but al-Ālūsī says its reliability is unknown.
rows.anchor: مياه الأرض كلها تتفجر من تحت صخرته والله تعالى أعلم بصحة ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says the Dajjāl cannot enter four mosques: Medina, Mecca, al-Aqṣā, and Sinai; al-Aqṣā is also one of three mosques to which journeys are specially made.
rows.anchor: وهو أحد المساجد الثلاث التي تشد إليها الرحال والأربع التي يمنع دخولها الدجال

rows.speaker: ميمونة مولاة رسول الله
rows.claim: Maymūna reports the Prophet called Bayt al-Maqdis the gathering and resurrection land and urged visiting and praying there, where a prayer counts as a thousand.
rows.anchor: أرض المحشر والمنشر ائتوه وصلوا فيه فإن صلاة فيه بألف صلاة
